problem.passage:
In any case it was dangerous, and an abomination that ought to have been done away with. Well, I was close to the edge of this hollow--there being a short cut to the Manchester road just beyond it--when Philip overtook me. He didn’t spare me, I can tell you, for, apart from the money question, there was an old sore between us. The girl he wanted to marry had done me the honour to prefer his father’s confidential clerk. She was a sensible girl, and saw the point to which our lives were drifting. When he had called me reptile, and a few other equally agreeable names, finding that he couldn’t sting me into retaliation by abuse of that kind, he came close up to me and struck me across the face with his open hand.

Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Philip in the text?

problem.passage:
"Meet me at breakfast alone,
And then I will give you a dish
Which really deserves to be known,
Though 'tis not the genteelest of fish.
You must promise to come, for I said
A splendid red herring I'd buy.
Nay, turn not aside your proud head;
You'll like it, I know, when you try.

"If moisture the herring betray,
Drain till from the moisture 'tis free.
Warm it through in the usual way,
Then serve it for you and for me.
A piece of cold butter prepare,
To rub it when ready it lies;
Egg sauce and potatoes don't spare,
And the flavour will cause you surprise."

Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward the red herring?

problem.passage:
Were we framed merely that we might for a few years rejoice in the beauty of the stars, as in that of the flowers beneath our feet? And ought we to be grateful for those transitory glimpses of the heavens, as for the fading splendour of the earth? But the heavens are not an idle show, hung out for the gaze of that idle dreamer Man. They are the work of the Eternal God, and He has given us power therein to read and to understand His glory. It is not our eyes only that are dazzled by the face of heaven--our souls can comprehend the laws by which that face is overspread by its celestial smiles. The dwelling-place of our spirits is already in the heavens.

Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward the heavens?

Last night we heard the calls of natives at the opposite side of the river. As soon as they saw us, they crossed the river, and came pretty close to us: the discharge of our guns, however, kept them at a distance. Several of our party, during their watches saw them moving with fire sticks on the other side of the river. In the morning, three of them came boldly up; so I went to them with some presents, and they became very friendly indeed. Presents were exchanged; and they invited us in the most pressing manner to accompany them to their camp; and were evidently disappointed in finding that we could not swim.

I hasten to write, and beg you, as far as I am concerned, to pay no attention whatever to it. He was sent over to us by Lady Heton, a traveling acquaintance, whom we know really nothing of, and it's been a great bother trying to be civil and everything else to him. I felt obliged to give him the letter, but you will understand by this that you are to ignore it quite as much as you like. He is no friend of ours whatever, merely an acquaintance that has been forced upon us.

At the end of June we had again dropped back to eleventh. At the end of July we had climbed up to eighth, and at the end of August we were sixth, having then climbed into the first division. As he put aside his coat and hat and entered her room, it seemed to him that he had forever put aside all else of essay and ambition beyond those four walls. problem.passage:
The truth is, that when a guest, of no matter how agreeable a presence, or how attractive an air, has made up his mind to go, the sooner he goes the better. Let him go at once, therefore. Do not press him to stay, or detain him at the door, but “speed” him on his way. It is best for both parties, if they like each other. When, indeed, an unpleasant intruder is about to depart, there is a kind of satisfaction in detaining him a little. We dally with the prospective pleasure of having him gone, till we forget that he is present. But when those we love are leaving us, the best way is, to wink, and part at once; for to be “going” is even worse than to be “gone.”

Based on the text, why does the writer advise parting quickly from loved ones?

On the day of the fire my constitution succumbed to a severe cold, caused by undue exertion in getting ready to do something. problem.explanation: 지문은 배가 'in the mid sea'에서 갑자기 멈췄다고 하므로 실제 육지에 걸린 것이 아니다. 선원들이 노를 젓고 돛을 더 펼쳐도 'all in vain'이었다는 점에서, 이 비유는 배가 땅에 고정된 듯 꼼짝 않고 멈춘 상태를 뜻한다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 'fast'를 속도로 오해한 것이고, C는 바다 한가운데라는 설정과 맞지 않으며, D는 갑작스러운 정지를 점진적 감속으로 바꾸어 틀리다.

problem.passage:
One can always see trouble who looks for it. I had never been across the plains and before the time for the train to start I walked to the front of the engine and looking along the track as it reached out across the prairie I saw trouble. What was it? Why, six miles ahead the track wasn't wide enough. Yes, I saw it. Then on six miles more the rails came together, with my destination nineteen hundred miles away. Soon the train moved and as we neared the difficulty, the track opened to welcome us. Not a pin was torn up nor a rail displaced. Again I looked ahead and a mountain was on the track, but before I had time to get off the mountain got off.

Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

From cheerful confidence about the trip to deep regret over a missed destination
From quiet boredom with the prairie to angry frustration at the slow train
From calm curiosity about the engine to grim fear of a coming accident

problem.passage:
Is your world a small one, made unendurable by a thousand petty cares? Are the heart and soul of you cast down by bitter disappointment? Would you leave it all, if only for an hour, and come back with a new point of view? Then open the covers of a book.

With this gentle comrade, you may journey to the very end of the world and even to the beginning of civilisation. There is no land which you may not visit, from Arctic snows to the loftiest peaks of southern mountains. Gallant gentlemen will go with you and tell you how to appreciate what you see.

Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

problem.passage:
Three honest generations of us have kept it clean and honorable, and our wives have done the same for us all down to you--all except my wife. I used to think that in marrying me you had placed me deeper in your debt than I could ever repay. Ever since the first time I saw you I loved you; and after that meeting I put my arms about no woman--arms that had been free enough before--until I put them around you. And since then the same. I have been an absolutely faithful husband to you. Do you understand what that means? I don't believe so. I preferred you to every other woman in the world.

Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

problem.passage:
I threw out my arms, expecting to catch the living body of some person; but not so--I caught nothing. As I turned round I felt the same touch on my right cheek. It might have been imagination, but I thought I again heard Lottie calling my name. The truth is, I was so much overcome with excitement that I scarcely knew what was going on around me. Harry was out but a few moments, returning accompanied by the fireman, who immediately lighted the lamp. We procured a lantern and began to search for the mysterious passenger. We carefully examined every seat, looking under each bench, but could find nobody. We went out and examined the rear platform, thinking that probably some one might be stealing a ride, but nothing of the sort was to be seen.

Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

problem.passage:
Washington Flagg was gone, but his shadow was to linger for a while longer on our household. It was difficult to realize that the weight which had oppressed us had been removed. A month or two after his disappearance an incident occurred which brought him back very vividly and in a somewhat sinister shape to our imaginations. Quite late one night there was a sharp ring at the door. Mary having gone to bed, I answered the bell.

problem.passage:
I went mad, mad, I really did. I made up my mind to have a house I could live in comfortably, and I was generous enough to let my husband have something he liked too. Do you know, before he married me, fond as he was of his pictures and china and things, it had never occurred to him to build a place to put them in? But I changed all that. I practically rebuilt the house, as you see; let in a little light and air into the musty corners; let him have a gallery which has become the joy of his heart.

problem.passage:
Ye dwell beside our paths and homes,
Our paths of sin, our homes of sorrow,
And guilty man, where'er he roams,
Your innocent mirth may borrow.
The birds of air before us fleet,
They cannot brook our shame to meet--
But we may taste your solace sweet,
And come again to-morrow.

Ye fearless in your nests abide--
Nor may we scorn, too proudly wise,
Your silent lessons undescried
By all but lowly eyes;
For ye could draw th' admiring gaze
Of Him who worlds and hearts surveys:
Your order wild, your fragrant maze,
He taught us how to prize.

Which choice best describes the speaker's attitude toward the flowers addressed in the poem?

problem.passage:
Having received nothing, I have nothing to give. Fortunately, the only thing of importance to be said this evening can be said without technical knowledge of any kind. The School of Art needs better accommodation. The financial details will be explained to you by those who are more conversant with them than I am. I will only say that parsimony in this matter on the part of the government or other public bodies will, in my humble opinion, be unwise. I am not for a lavish expenditure of public money, even on education. It would be a misfortune if parental duty were to be cast on the State, and parents were to be allowed to forget that they are bound to provide their children with education as well as with bread.

problem.passage:
Is the best Gothic fit for our worship? Does it express our belief? Or shall we choose some other style?

I say that it is; and that it is so because it is a style which, if not founded on Nature, has taken into itself more of Nature, of Nature beautiful and healthy, than any other style.

With greater knowledge of Nature, both geographical and scientific, fresh styles of architecture may and will arise, as much more beautiful, and as much more natural, than the Gothic, as Gothic is more beautiful and natural than the Norman. Till then we must take the best models which we have; use them; and, as it were, use them up and exhaust them.

Time passed on, and the Fairies had done nothing to gain their lovely home again. They wept no longer, but watched little Bud, as she daily tended the flowers, restoring their strength and beauty, or with gentle words flew from nest to nest, teaching the little birds to live happily together; and wherever she went blessings fell, and loving hearts were filled with gratitude.

Flowers looked lovingly up as they passed, birds sang to cheer them when sad thoughts made them weep. And soon little Bud found out their gentle deeds, and her friendly words gave them new strength.

problem.passage:
If Richard prayed, it was with the heart, for his lips never opened. But I believe that his heart, in this hour of clear defeat, was turned to stone. He took his joys with riot, his triumphs calmly; his griefs he shut in a trap. Such a nature as his, I suppose, respects no persons. Whether God beat him, or his enemy, he would take it the same way. All that Gilles heard him say aloud was this: 'What I have done I have done: deliver us from evil.' He bade no farewell to his hope, he asked no greeting for his altered way. Doubtless, in their jungle-lairs, the wise old gray-beards put their heads together and agreed to raise the price on pennies when the worthless gold was all worked off. Who could tell? "See, Winter comes, to rule the varied year,
Sullen and sad, with all his rising train,
Vapours, and clouds, and storms. Be these my theme,
These! that exalt the soul to solemn thought,
And heavenly musing. Welcome, kindred glooms!
Congenial horrors, hail! with frequent foot,
Pleased have I, in my cheerful morn of life,
When nursed by careless Solitude I lived,
And sung of Nature with unceasing joy,
Pleased have I wander'd through your rough domain;
Trod the pure virgin-snows, myself as pure;
Heard the winds roar, and the big torrents burst;
Or seen the deep-fermenting tempest brew'd
In the grim evening sky. Thus passed the time,
Till through the lucid chambers of the south
Look'd out the joyous Spring, look'd out, and smiled!"

problem.passage:
The chamber of the solitary student is peopled with immortal guests. He has friends who are always steadfast, who are never false, who are silent when he is weary, who go forth with him to his work, who await his return. In the literature of the world a grand society is open to all who choose to enter it.

Books are the chief food of our intellectual life.--There are men that have, indeed, done great things who have read but little. These have had their want of mental training compensated by their powers of observation and experience of life. But they have been for the most part exceptional men, and it is possible they might have done better if they had studied more.

problem.passage:
With a firm step he walked from his prison to the foot of the gibbet, and mounted the steps. Resting a moment, he addressed the spectators, exhorting them to take example from his dreadful fate, and to avoid the evil courses which had, step by step, conducted him to it. At length the executioner warned him that his time was up.

"I am ready," he answered, and was about to submit his neck to the fatal noose, when, starting back, he exclaimed in a voice of agony, "He is come! he is come! Oh, save me from him!--save me!"

Before he could utter more, the drop was let fall, and all was soon over. The rest of the crew died making no sign.

problem.passage:
Suppose thrown among us a person of well-developed intellect, but unacquainted with a single language or word that we use. It is absolutely useless to talk to him, because nothing that we say conveys any meaning to his mind. We can supply him no dictionary, because by hypothesis he knows no language to which we have access. How shall we proceed to communicate our ideas to him? Clearly there is but one possible way--namely, through his senses. Outside of this means of bringing him in contact with us we can have no communication with him. We, therefore, begin by showing him sensible objects, and letting him understand that certain words which we use correspond to those objects.

Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude in the text?

In fact, civilization from its very inception has been “machine-made.” It began when our remotest ancestor snatched the bough of a tree and decided thenceforth to walk erect, using the bough as staff and club--that is, as a machine. Because the machine represents the effort of man to adjust himself to his environment, his environment to himself.

The mystical element in him was for ever reaching out in search of some Divine essence in the world. He was not in search at any time of personal relations. He attracted more affection than he ever gave; he rejoiced its sympathy and kindred companionship as a flower rejoices in sunshine; but I think he had little taste of the baffled suffering which accompanies all deep human passion. We never reached the far wall that summer, though Dario spoke of it each morning as if distance were only another word to learn. He sat on the rim of the salt pool in Havana, trousers rolled, and named things in the language of his village: tile, gull, the green rust on the ladder. Bartolo repeated each word and swam a length before the next. On Thursday she stopped short of the far wall, held the rope, and came back saying she had only wanted to rest. Dario nodded and gave her the word for rest, then a second, older word that he said meant resting before one has finished. She practiced it without asking why. Later, reciting the colors, he paused at the word for the rust, and let her supply it, which she did loudly, as though he had been testing her. On the walk home she carried his towel over her shoulder, still damp at one corner where the rope had dripped on it.

leans the way it leaned when she wrote out sums.

Is a delay a kind of confessional? So I wondered at the ferry terminal in Thessaloniki, where weather held the steamer two days and a gentleman named Emre took the bench beside mine. He was bound for a dying friend and could not decide whether to tell him that his son had sold the family vineyard. He decided aloud, hourly, in a fog of cheap tobacco, beginning each round with "Miss Edith, consider." I wrote in my notebook that he talked as a gull walks, much and to no end, and showed the line to the clerk, who laughed. I was not mocking him, exactly, or not only. On the second morning the porter offered me the ladies' waiting room, which was quiet and warm, and I said I preferred the draught. When the steamer was at last called, Emre had still settled nothing, and somewhere between the bench and the gangway the page with the gull on it went into the harbor.

Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Emre as conveyed in the text?

Four rules governed the bakery in Chengdu before dawn: flour first, then water, then salt, then silence. Dalia had learned them at fourteen, when her aunt took her in, and for three years the two of them had folded dough side by side without speaking, her aunt's knuckles pressing a pattern that Dalia copied stroke for stroke. Each morning her aunt set out two aprons on the counter, though Dalia owned three of her own. Dalia never asked why. That winter her aunt's wrists swelled, and one morning she did not come down. Dalia worked alone. She weighed the flour, poured the water, measured the salt. When the first trays were out, she found that she had set two aprons on the counter herself, and that between folds she had been pausing for knuckles beside hers that did not come. She took the second apron and hung it back on its hook.

Years later the tenants of the block in Nairobi would still describe Ren tapping the rooftop water tank each dawn with a spanner, three knocks, listening for how full it rang. Moshe, the surveyor sent by the water board, watched him do it on his first morning and noted in his ledger that the meter had been broken for a decade. Ren nodded. He showed Moshe where the overflow pipe rusted, where pigeons drank, where the children hid their kites. In a corner of the roof sat a folded canvas bag that neither man mentioned. On Moshe's final morning he brought a new meter, installed it, and read the numbers aloud. Ren listened, then picked up the spanner, knocked three times on the tank, and handed the spanner to the boy from the third floor who had come up to watch. Then he lifted the canvas bag onto his shoulder.

By the time we stopped at the diner outside Krakow, the commission was gone: the church restorers had chosen another workshop, and Matthias said it was because my joints on the sample pew had gapped. I agreed. I had measured too fast. Over pierogi and weak coffee he listed my errors, calmly, the way he listed lumber, and I wrote them on a napkin. On the windowsill beside our booth stood a small carved bird with one wing mended in a darker wood; neither of us spoke of it. A year later, sorting his papers when his eyes failed, I found the restorers' letter. They had praised the pew. They had chosen the other workshop because Matthias asked a price he must have known they could not pay. I drove out to the diner again. I ordered pierogi and weak coffee, and I left the napkin, still folded, under my cup.

problem.passage:
Who teaches scales on a bridge in February? Budi did, every Thursday of my fourteenth year, marching me from his flat to the stone span over the canal so that, he said, I could hear the note without a room to flatter it. He stopped me at every sour interval. He would tap the parapet twice, and I would begin again while barges slid underneath and my fingers went white. On the last of those Thursdays he set a coin on the stone and walked off without collecting it. Then he was gone: no letter, no forwarding address, eleven years. When he reappeared one spring, he gave no account of where he had been. I was teaching by then, and on a cold Thursday I had brought my own pupil to the same bridge, telling her that a room would only flatter her. Budi stood a little way off and listened through two scales. He did not tap the parapet once. When we finished, he nodded at my pupil, then at me, and went to buy chestnuts.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

On his final morning I turned my stool around, so that it faced the church, and sat there until he came.

Years later, the binder on Peitavas Street still remembered the gardener who came in with a ledger wrapped in sacking. Stanislav had kept that book for the old owner of the house on the hill for thirty-one seasons, writing each planting in a narrow hand and heading every page with the owner's initials, as he had been taught. The spine is splitting, he told the binder; it will not last another winter. That was true. He had carried it in the week after the new owner, Marta, signed for the house, and not before, though the spine had been splitting for years. He asked that the old pages be resewn exactly as they were. Then he asked for forty blank leaves to be added behind them. When the book was ready, he did not take it to his shed. He walked it up the hill, set it on Marta's kitchen table, and laid his pencil across the first empty page.

Saturdays belong to the market. Renata pushes the wheelchair between the stalls, and her mother, who has called her señora since the wedding, points with her cane at what she will not eat. Not the yuca; it is for other people's kitchens. Not the black beans; her own mother made lentils. Renata pays for both anyway and hangs the bags on the chair's handles. At home there is one table and two ways of setting it, and on alternate Sundays the lentils win. This week the coin purse her mother keeps inside her sleeve is lighter by the price of a pound of beans, and the bag Renata finds on the counter, knotted the old way, was not bought by Renata. Her mother says nothing about it. At dinner she lays the lentil spoon in the drawer and sets the ladle beside Renata's pot, handle turned toward her own plate.

Above the warehouses of the Speicherstadt, on a roof reached by forty-one steps, the washing line of Remedios and Wolfram has hung for nineteen years. He splices it fresh each spring, as sailmakers once did, tucking the strands under and over while she holds the far end and watches his hands. Neither of them says much. He does not explain the tucks; she does not ask. On ordinary Mondays she pegs out sheets, and he takes his shirts down before dark. Their friendship is a line strung with pegs and little else, swaying between two chimneys in the harbor wind. This spring his fingers were slow, and he stopped halfway. Remedios took the loose strands from him, tucked the next three herself, crookedly, and he let the crooked ones stand.

Once, at dusk, I walked the soccer field in Bologna
with Ottavio, who had clerked for me the final year
before they took my robe and gave me a garden.
Still he called me Judge Fiorella, and still he carried
my late husband's whistle, the silver one,
polished and wrapped in a folded handkerchief,
and spoke of it as evidence: its dent, its chain,
the date engraved in letters small as rulings.
I answered him as I once answered counsel,
with thanks, with patience, with the proper phrases,
and asked him kindly if he meant to keep it.
He said it was mine.
The field was empty.
Lights came on.
A boy's ball rolled to the line and stopped.
I thanked him for his care.
I took the whistle from the cloth
and, still thanking him, blew it once
and sent the ball back to the boy.

Between lengths he taught her words from the language of his childhood, across the ocean: the word for cold water, the word for a river that bends, the word for someone who is late coming home. She repeated them to the tiles and forgot most of them by Tuesday. He would not say who had taught him to swim. In March, fetching his coat from the hook, she found a folded letter addressed to a woman whose name she did not know, written in that language, unsent and creased many times along the same lines. She could read three words of it: cold water, a river that bends, someone late coming home. The following Sunday she arrived at the pool before him, and she was already reciting to the tiles when he came through the door.

Which choice best states the main idea of the passage?

Three rules governed the wall between Kwesi's beekeeper's yard and Kwame's house in Dakar: no climbing, no smoke on windy days, and no talk of the photograph. Kwame kept the picture in a frame, a print of two boys on one bicycle beside a row of hives against that same wall, and each morning he hung it in his window facing the yard. Years ago Kwesi had moved his hives to the far corner, saying the bees disliked the afternoon heat by the wall, and he worked there with his back to the window. In the dry season of 1987, Kwame's son mentioned at the well that his father now read the newspaper with a glass and no longer crossed the street alone. That same week Kwesi began moving the hives back, one each evening after dark, telling anyone who asked that the far corner flooded in the rains. By March the last hive stood under the window, humming. Each morning Kwesi set a jar of the first honey on top of the wall, its lid loosened.

Three rules governed the old weaving house in Lisbon, and you learned them on your first day: no lamp after midnight, no cloth cut before it is finished, and no news spoken until it is certain. Rafaela, who had bought the house that winter, kept all three. Each morning she climbed to the loom room while Mateo, the gardener, pruned the lemon trees below, and each morning she wove one more row of a blue cloth with no pattern anyone could name. The ship carrying her brother was weeks overdue. When Mateo asked why she did not weave something useful, a shawl or a blanket, she only said that the cloth was not finished. Rows gathered like days. Once, when a rumor of a wreck came up the hill, her hands stopped above the threads for a full hour; then she tied the next knot and went on. By midsummer, Mateo had begun bringing her a sprig of lemon blossom each dawn and laying it, without a word, beside the growing blue.

I interpreted for Pavel, a Czech engineer hired to inspect the old signal lamp, which now guided nothing but the fishing boats that crossed the reservoir at night. By the fourth day, though, I had watched him wait on that landing for hours, his notebook open to blank pages, while the keepers drank tea below and shrugged. I took the last night bus out of Marseille with my violin across my knees and, in my coat pocket, the cake of rosin Remy had given me at my first lesson. It was cracked down the middle now, worn into a shallow valley by eight years of his insistence that I bow slower, slower. The audition in Paris was in the morning, and the teacher there had already written that he used only a newer, softer rosin; he would supply it. Twice, as the bus wound along the coast, I took Remy's cake out, meaning to leave it on the seat beside me. Twice I put it back. Somewhere past Aix, I rubbed my thumb along the crack until it was warm, and I did not sleep. The windows showed only my own reflection, and behind it, the dark.

Hortense obeyed, as she had obeyed in Ivy's classroom thirty years before. The bees grew sluggish and mild, and Ivy lifted out a heavy frame without a single sting. Now, watching the drowsy bees surrender their honey, she wondered what else had been lifted out of that house while she was busy chewing. Three rules my uncle Dewi kept at the loom:
count every thread, owe no one, trust no rival.
We owed the cooperative in Bologna
more than a winter's linen could repay,
and Nora, at the next loom, wove faster than us both.
He called her the competition. I called her nothing.
But when our warp snapped on the morning of the market,
it was Nora who knotted it, thread across thread,
her weft running sideways through our long, straight lines.
Warp holds still; weft crosses over.
Neither one alone is cloth.
By evening the bolt was finished, and my uncle,
counting, lost his place, and laughed, and counted again.

Three weeks earlier he had hidden among the rope lockers on my boat, and so he had seen, as no one else had, the moment I, Leah, misjudged the tide and scraped the pier. "They'll ask me tomorrow," he said. "At the hearing. What do I say?" My stomach tightened; I had rehearsed a gentler version of that night so many times it almost felt true. But I looked at him, sixteen and soaked through, and told him to say exactly what he saw, every second of it, and that I would say the same. He nodded slowly. At Ardwick a woman boarded carrying a sleeping terrier wrapped in a scarf.

We set type side by side there for nine years before he moved to Goa, and he still calls me, Ishaan, his apprentice, though I outlasted him by a decade. I keep picturing the foreman tapping each line of type with his thumb, proud as a father, and I am not sure what I will say. Bergen in July smelled of tar and wet lilac, and the long dining hall of the summer school where I worked as a boy smelled of both. I was the gardener's son, trimming hedges for Thorvald, who had bought the estate that spring. One evening he called me in while the students ate and announced, before all of them, that he would pay my fees at the cathedral school in autumn. My face burned; I was holding a rake, and my boots had left a trail across his clean floor. Yet when he shook my hand, his grip was so earnest that I forgot the boots, and I thanked him twice, the second time louder. Jens, my father, was waiting by the kitchen door. Through the windows, gulls wheeled above the fish market.

Keep it, she said, pressing it into his bag. A year is too long to wait for some things. Jakub said nothing, but at the station he wound it carefully and set it to her time. Snow drifted against the shop window long after the train had gone, and the wall clocks struck noon together.

two old rivals, the game between us set down.

For a whole term I had not said one word in your class, and you had stopped calling on me, which I took as a judgment. Then the bus stalled on the bridge, and you turned around and asked whether anyone had a pencil to lend a man who wanted to write down the lights on the water. I handed you mine. We talked until the engine caught again, mostly about poems I had never shown anyone. I think now that my silence was never indifference, only a kind of waiting. Here the rain has not stopped for days, and the gulls sleep on the ferry railings.
Despina

I watched Katharina unwrap the brooch
beside a cup of coffee going cold,
the Hamburg trains exhaling on the platform
like tired men setting down their coats.
Her husband's, she said, pinned each winter
to the collar he wore for every leaving.
My hands, a bride's hands, were not certain
what a newcomer is owed of the dead,
or whether I had any right to touch it.
But she slid it over the marble tabletop
slowly, the way one offers bread to a sparrow,
and smiled the small smile of a woman
who has practiced letting go in private.
I held it until the metal warmed,
until it seemed, almost, to hold me back,
and Katharina's hand rested on my wrist.
Outside, a whistle; somewhere a door;
the waiter brushing crumbs into his palm.

I boarded Albert's barge on the Irwell expecting to stay ten minutes. Thirty years earlier he had torn my essay in half before the whole class, and I had carried that sound with me ever since. Now he moved slowly between coils of rope, offering tea in a chipped mug, and I kept my coat buttoned and my answers short. He did not apologize. Instead he showed me a shoebox of student papers he had kept, and mine was near the top, taped carefully along its tear. I set the mug down without drinking. Still, when he struggled with the stove, I reached over and lit it for him, and I did not leave when the ten minutes were up. Gulls settled on the roof of the cabin, and the water knocked against the hull.

the Cornish wind half wrestling them from me,
and laughed to think how many years we'd spent
at chess-club boards, two old men keeping score

each losing move of mine marked out in ink
and next to it, in his small careful hand,
the better move, and then: "Show Mabel this."

with one white sheet held open in my arms

the Lima heat pressing through the high windows,
and I in my borrowed white, braced
for Renata, Santiago's mother,
who had said, the week before, that I was too young
to know what I was promising.
I had rehearsed my answers to her like a debate.
But when the sound system shrieked and died
and the aunts began to murmur,
it was Renata who climbed onto a bench,
her good shoes in one hand,
and sang the first hymn without a microphone
until the whole room followed.
Later she pinned my slipping veil
with a clip from her own hair
and told me, gruffly, that she had been too young once, too.
I keep that clip in a dish by the door.
I still do not know all her reasons.
I know whose voice filled the room
when mine would not come.

Who measures salt by the sound it makes
falling into a pot? Soren did,
old captain, on the promenade bench,
explaining his fish stew to the gulls
and to Leah, who had once hidden
in his hold among the potato sacks
and been found, and fed, and never sent back.
A handful of this. Enough of that.
Until it smells like the harbor at Newlyn
the morning after a storm.
Such instructions are useless, of course.
No cook could follow them.
And still she leans close, notebook shut,
learning the way he tilts his wrist,
the pause he takes before the pepper,
as if the recipe were a weather
only the body could forecast.
Below them the tide pulls the sand smooth
and writes nothing on it either.

Three times Tendai invited me to supper, and three times I refused, each time with a reason that sounded better on the stair than it had in my head. We shared a wall, Tendai and I, in a narrow house near the Company's Garden, and through that wall I heard her sing while she cooked, badly and with great happiness. I told myself I was too busy. Who keeps a ledger in a post office drawer?

of the little office on the edge of Rotterdam,

and tore out the page that bore my name.
"Anneke," he said, "I was keeping the wrong account."
Now the stamps look softer in the window light,
and the brass scale, for once, weighs nothing at all.

“I won't be coming to the anniversary dinner,” Bahram said, moving his bishop before Tamar had finished setting the board. They had played on this hillside terrace above Dhaka every Friday for twenty-two years, and for twenty-two years Bahram had won exactly as often as he lost. Now he studied his old rival's face and saw, for the first time, a tremor in the hand that held the bishop. Bahram's eyes had been failing for months; he could no longer read a menu, let alone a speech. Tamar said nothing about it. Kingston wakes slowly at the roadside diner,
where Errol orders for his son without asking
and Hemi lets him, the way one lets weather happen.
All morning on the hill road the father led,
his old knees steady as a pair of oars,
until, a stone's throw from the painted line,
he bent to fix a shoe that needed no fixing.
Now Hemi turns the ribbon in his fingers
and says the shoe was tied. Errol says, eat.
Hemi does not eat. He watches the hands
that taught him how to grip a cricket bat,
how to lose a game without kicking the dust,
and thinks there must be a way to lose
that costs a man more than winning would.
Outside, a truck of breadfruit idles at the pump,
its driver singing to no one in particular.

After eleven months under Bogdan's roof, I, Bronislaw, could list his habits the way other boys listed saints: the pencil behind the left ear, the refusal to sand before noon, the low whistle when a board surprised him. Its doors did not meet. I laughed before I could stop myself, and he laughed too, longer than I did. On the drive home I kept the photograph on my knee. I had thought his skill was something he had been handed, like the color of his eyes. In the workshop that week I found myself measuring every cut twice, and once, for no reason I could name, a third time. Bogdan noticed and said nothing, though he moved his own pencil to the right ear.

Storms make liars of us all. So I told myself that night in the hospital waiting room in Accra, where the rain had driven half the street indoors and the lamps flickered as if embarrassed. Obinna went quiet. He told me, slowly, that his brother lay somewhere among them, and that he had never once gone to look. I sat beside him and did not speak of tea again.
